title: Brain tuberculoma in a non-endemic area
case_text: A 24 year-old man who had immigrated from Ethiopia six years prior presented to our Emergency Department with intermittent left leg shaking for two days. His left leg felt tired and he was reluctant to stand on it. He was previously healthy and had no history of fever, chills, night sweats, or weight loss. He was well appearing with no abnormal findings on physical and neurological examination. A computed tomography (CT) scan showed right frontoparietal edema. A contrast-enhanced scan was performed, revealing an associated frontoparietal enhancing mass. magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain demonstrated a 2.6x1.6 cm mass with surrounding edema (Figure 1). CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed periceliac and peiraortic lymphadenopathy, and questionable but no definitive pulmonary nodules. Having received the Bacillus Calmette-Guerin vaccine, his tuberculin sensitivity test was positive. He was started on levetiracetam for treatment of simple partial seizures, and dexamethasone for treatment of vasogenic edema. He underwent right parietal craniotomy with intraoperative monitoring for resection of the lesion and tissue diagnosis. The underlying dura was soft and uninvolved. Opening the dura revealed a superficial mass with well defined margins that easily peeled away from the underlying parenchyma (Figure 2). Pathological examination demonstrated necrotizing granulomas with peripheral palisading epithelioid histiocytes, giant cells, and acid fast bacilli, consistent with cerebral tuberculoma (Figure 3). Blood cultures and HIV testing were negative. Following surgery, he had no neurological deficits and had no further seizure activity. He was rapidly tapered from steroids and continued on levetiracetam for an additional month. He completed a six-month regimen of isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrizinamide, and was doing well without neurological sequelae five months after completion of therapy.

You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Tuberculosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: cerebral tuberculoma
